articles.title: The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild review
articles.summary: Link’s latest adventure is a bold and much-needed reinvention of the beloved franchise
articles.body: The moment I realized The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild might actually be my favorite Zelda adventure ever struck me like lightning — literally. While running through the picturesque green fields of Hyrule, a massive storm unexpectedly rolled in. As heavy rain began to pour, a strong wind rustled the tall grass, and in the distance I could hear the crack of lightning. The sharp sound rapidly came closer and closer until zap! I was electrocuted to death by a bolt. Every time I restarted, the same thing would happen. I couldn’t understand why the lightning was targeting me, the helpless hero, until I realized that both the spear and shield on my back were made of metal. With the steel unequipped, I was able to safely make my through the storm. Breath of the Wild has something that’s been missing from the series for years: surprise. Most recent Zelda adventures have become formulaic, abiding by a rigid and proven structure that offers nostalgia and familiarity, but little room for revelations, either big or small. Breath of the Wild is more open and natural than its predecessors, letting you discover things — like how lightning works — through experimentation. It isn’t always as curated and cinematic as other Zelda games, but the unpredictability makes it feel like a true adventure, where you’re uncovering your own path, instead of hitting your marks and following the script. Zelda games have always been large, but Breath of the Wild feels uniquely grand, a massive open world filled with so much to do that I suspect most players — even those who complete the main story — will miss large swaths of the map. The scale could have been daunting, but the joy of discovery and the satisfaction that comes from finding your own way make it inviting instead. I want to go the places I’ve yet to discover. I want to uncover new secrets and abilities. I want more. At 50 hours into the game, I still haven’t reached the end of Breath of the Wild. In some ways it feels like I’ve only scratched the surface. But even still, these bold changes have profoundly altered my expectations of what a Zelda adventure can be. And I’m entirely convinced that this is the best Zelda game I’ve ever played. This review contains light spoilers for the early hours of Breath of the Wild. [Image: Breath of the Wild opens with series hero Link awakening in a dark cavern. A mysterious disembodied voice guides him to a tablet that has a passing resemblance to both the Switch and Nintendo’s maligned Wii U controller. The tablet helps to navigate this version of Hyrule — the fantasy realm that has long been the heart of Zelda adventures. As you learn in the very early parts of the game, a century ago, powerful evil destroyed much of the world, allowing nature to reclaim castles, and littering the land with abandoned machines of war. People still exist, in small towns and stables, but much of Hyrule is beset by hordes of monsters who have bivouacked into the hills. This is a dangerous place. Naturally, your job is to set things right. One of the game’s greatest strengths is how it goes about explaining how you will do that — or just as often, not explaining it. Breath of the Wild rarely gives you explicit directions as to what to do. Instead, it tells (or shows) you what needs to happen, and lets you fill in the rest. One line of quests tasks you with uncovering shrines (more on those later) using only lines from a poem or a riddle as guidance. Another presents a series of images of scenic Hyrule locations from before the calamity, and asks you to find them as they are now. In order to defeat Ganon you’ll need to first uncover four “divine beasts” scattered throughout the world. Of course, the game doesn’t even tell you what a divine beast is. This lack of direction can be disorienting at first. I played Breath of the Wild immediately after finishing another huge role-playing game, Horizon Zero Dawn, and it was a jarring transition. After spending 40 hours playing a game that literally pointed me in the right direction at all times, now I was forced to fend for myself. But it very quickly turned into a liberating sensation. Instead of worrying if I was following the correct path, for the first dozen hours or so, I largely ignored the story altogether. Instead, I trekked across Hyrule activating the specific towers found in each region, which not only help fill in the details of the map but also provide crucial fast-travel points. Even the act of filling out Breath of the Wild’s map instils a deep sense of adventure. In most open-world games, particularly Ubisoft titles like Far Cry or Assassin’s Creed, your map is overburdened with icons from the very beginning. You can spot where everything from a city to a treasure chest is located before you even start exploring. It can feel overwhelming. Breath of the Wild, meanwhile, does the opposite. When you first start out, the map is almost completely empty. You can see the dividing lines between the various regions that make up Hyrule, but none of their details. It’s only once you start exploring that it fills out. A town won’t appear on your map until you actually go there, which you can only do by finding it on your own. Discovering a new place or thing truly feels like an act of discovery. [Image: Breath of the Wild features two significant additions that completely changed how I viewed the world around me. In addition to the usual methods of traversal — foot, horse, and fast travel — Link now also has the ability to climb nearly every surface you come across. If you spot a mountain, a castle, or virtually anything else, you can climb it. The only restriction is Link’s stamina — which expands over time and can be augmented with things like potions — but even then there are ways around it if you’re clever. This marks a fundamental shift for the series. Instead of an impediment, walls and mountains are now just another potential pathway. Often I would bypass monster-plagued roads altogether and simply climb the comparatively safe mountain instead. Link’s climbing ability is made all the more useful and important by a seemingly innocuous paraglider, which lets Link temporarily soar through the air. In short order, it became a pivotal part of the game, and my main method of transportation. Instead of walking or riding to a new location, I would climb the nearest high point — a mountain, or maybe a tower — and then glide in the direction of where I wished to be. The act of getting somewhere became exciting in and of itself. There’s a certain pleasure that comes from just having enough energy to reach the top of a tower before losing your grip, or sailing peacefully above enemy camps as the monsters sleep below, unaware. Not only is Breath of the Wild’s map large; it’s also dense. I was constantly discovering new places and puzzles, both elaborate and diminutive. One of my favorite additions to the game is the shrines — glowing caverns scattered liberally across the map. Each one is like a miniature, self-contained Zelda dungeon. Early on these shrines serve as tutorials, showing necessary details about Link’s powers — like his ability to temporarily halt time or use bombs — but later they essentially become puzzle boxes, which approach Portal-levels of cleverness. The shrines also simplify the Zelda dungeon formula in an almost mobile game-like manner, resulting in satisfyingly quick puzzles that can usually be completed in less than 15 minutes or so. Even better, unlike typical Zelda puzzles, those in Breath of the Wild’s shrines often have multiple solutions. Many other additions help bring Breath of the Wild in line with contemporary open-world games like The Witcher or Skyrim, while also contributing to its overwhelming focus on adventure and discovery. Link can now cook, for instance, gathering ingredients in the wild, using them to make food that replenishes health or buffs abilities. I found myself especially taken with this feature, scouring the world for new vegetables and meats, and seeing what I could make of them. Again, cooking isn’t really explained, making it all the more compelling. Whipping up a tasty mushroom rice ball or meat-stuffed pumpkin using guesswork instead of a recipe is satisfying. I especially love the way ingredients dance and jump in the pot as you prepare a meal. There are also survival elements, forcing you to protect Link from extreme heat and cold. You’ll often find him shivering or sweating because of the weather, his health depleting. Weapons, too, give way. For the first time in a Zelda game your swords and shields degrade as you use them. But weapons are everywhere. You can even pick up a downed skeleton’s arm to bludgeon beasts, its fingers still twitching as you swing it about. Using your best equipment becomes a risky choice, not an assumption. [Image: Even though Breath of the Wild introduces RPG-like elements such as crafting and a greater focus on gear, it’s missing a very distinct kernel of the genre: experience. In most RPGs, numbers determine almost everything you can do. If you’re a level 5 character in a typical RPG, you definitely don’t want to head into a dungeon filled with level 10 enemies, and there’s a whole range of items and abilities you can’t use until you grind long enough to meet the appropriate level. This effectively walls off large portions of the world until you’ve achieved a numerical level of success. Breath of the Wild scraps this logic. Link gets more health and stamina as you progress, and you can acquire stronger weapons and armor, but he never gets stronger himself. He doesn’t learn to swing a sword or shoot a bow any better. But you do. Breath of the Wild offers a more open and expansive world to explore, but it also demands more of its players than other Zeldas, forcing you to get better and smarter to survive. It’s the most challenging Zelda I’ve played in many years, but also the most satisfying. (Though it never approaches the daunting difficulty of games like Bloodborne or Dark Souls.) All of these many changes fundamentally alter the Zelda formula. But what’s perhaps most remarkable about Breath of the Wild is that it still feels like a Zelda adventure — and it’s more than just the familiar setting and characters, or the stirring rendition of the Zelda theme that plays in the background. Breath of the Wild may be the biggest Zelda game to date, but it’s also an experience that distills the essence of the series into something more pure. More recent Zelda games have become bogged down with needless hand holding, an overabundance of tutorials, and overly complicated narratives. Breath of the Wild gets away from that. It changes the Zelda formula in dramatic ways, yet paradoxically it feels more Zelda than almost any game in the series before. By going big and open, Breath of the Wild gets at the heart at what a Zelda game should be. This new direction, and shaking up of the age-old formula that has come to define the series, helps Breath of the Wild return to what made Zelda so beloved in the first place. More so than just about any game series, Zelda’s heart lies in exploration, that moment of seeing a towering mountain in the distance and realizing that eventually you’ll be able to reach the top. Breath of the Wild takes this idea, cuts out the fluff, and expands upon it. It pulls ideas from other games, like crafting or survival, yet makes them feel perfectly at home in its beloved universe. It’s exactly the Zelda game I’ve been waiting for. Just watch out for lightning. The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild launches March 3rd on Nintendo Switch and Wii U.

articles.title: Spotify’s AI DJ now takes requests
articles.summary: Spotify is allowing subscribers to use voice commands to control which songs are spat out by its AI DJ feature.
articles.body: Spotify is giving users more control over which songs are spat out by its AI DJ feature. Starting today, Spotify Premium subscribers can now use English voice commands to personalize what music they want DJ to play instead of relying on the ever-changing playlist that it curates based on their listening habits. Users can access these new capabilities by pressing and holding the ‘DJ’ button located in the bottom right corner when using the AI DJ feature and listening for a beep. Users can then verbally tell the DJ bot what they want to hear, such as “play me some electronic beats for a midday run,” or “surprise me with some indie tracks I’ve never heard before.” Prior to the update, this button would just randomly switch up whatever song you were currently listening to and didn’t allow users to control what would be played next. Now, Spotify says that users can direct it to play specific artists, genres, and moods. It also borrows some of the quirkier vibe-based music recommendations from the AI Playlist building feature that Spotify launched in beta last year, which creates a tracklist based on text prompts. For example, users can ask the AI DJ to “play me some music to soundtrack my life as a movie.” [Image: If you have a particular track in mind then it may be easier to play it directly, rather than hope that the AI DJ lines it up for you. This new voice command update is currently the only means for users to have any control over what tracks the AI DJ will play, however, which is a bit awkward if you’re using the feature in an environment where you can’t be chatty.

articles.title: Bruce Springsteen fan club founders say political fights, El-Sayed endorsement led to shutdown: report
articles.summary: Bruce Springsteen's endorsement of Michigan's senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed proved the final straw for the Spring-Nuts fan club founders as group shutters.
articles.body:
A Bruce Springsteen fan club couldn't escape the badlands and shuttered over political commentary.

Founded more than a decade ago, the "Spring-Nuts" Facebook group dedicated to The Boss noticed its 18,000 members were no longer focused on his music as they battled against "hateful" online discourse due to Springsteen's public stances and recent endorsement of Michigan's senator-elect, Abdul El-Sayed .

"As the world grew increasingly divisive, hostile, those tensions inevitably spilled into our little corner of the E Street world," founders Julie and Howie Chaz said in a statement posted on Sunday, Nov. 8, according to Asbury Park Press .

"What should have been respectful differences of opinion too often deteriorated into personal attacks, bullying, insults, and some genuinely vile and hateful rhetoric."

Springsteen embarked on the "Land of Hope and Dreams" tour earlier this year with the E Street Band and legendary guitarist Tom Morello .

The 20-date tour across North America was slated in response to President Donald Trump and the " No Kings " protests.

"We are living through dark, disturbing and dangerous times, but do not despair – the cavalry is coming," Springsteen said while announcing the tour on social media in February.

"We will be rocking your town in celebration and in defense of America – American democracy, American freedom, our American Constitution and our sacred American dream – all of which are under attack by our wannabe king and his rogue government in Washington, D.C."

He added, "Everyone, regardless of where you stand or what you believe in, is welcome – so come on out and join the United Free Republic of E Street Nation for an American spring of rock 'n' rebellion! I'll see you there!"

"Spring-Nuts" founder Howie Chaz admitted that as Springsteen became "more outspoken about his politics," the group administrators were tasked with a "difficult balancing act" of respecting "his absolute right" while maintaining an ethical online community.

"How could we be a Bruce Springsteen fan community trying to protect that harmony and camaraderie and ignore messages and statements coming directly from the very artist who brought us all together," Howie said.

Springsteen's November endorsement of El-Sayed as "a fighter for our American Constitution" was the final straw for admins.

"Mr. Sayed campaigned with Hasan Piker who openly made horrific statements that America deserved 9/11," Howie said.

"After a Michigan synagogue was attacked back in March, obviously an act of terrorism, Sayed rationalized it by saying 'Hurt people hurt people' standing right next to the antisemitic streamer Hasan Piker who made the despicable 9/11 statement."

His endorsement was "deeply disappointing to us, given our concerns as proud Jews," Julie and Howie said.

"We certainly don't believe Bruce intended for his message to make fans feel unwelcome. But very unfortunately, some of his fans appointed themselves the gatekeepers of who was and wasn't worthy of belonging in the E Street community."

While the group's annual Seaside Serenade and Spring-Nuts podcasts will continue under a different name, the group will rebrand with a focus on music in general, Howie told the Asbury Park Press.

"One thing we want to make absolutely clear is that Julie and I can NEVER thank Bruce Springsteen and the E Street Band enough for the decades of music, memories, inspiration, and absolute JOY they have brought into our lives," Howie said on Facebook.

"Bruce has been, and always will be, an enormous part of our personal story and journey. His music has been the soundtrack to so many of the most meaningful moments of our lives, and through Spring-Nuts, it opened doors, created opportunities, and introduced us to extraordinary people and experiences we could never have imagined."

Springsteen's representatives did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

articles.title: Hipnose no cinema: rede testa 'apagar' filmes da memória | G1
articles.standfirst: Empresa aposta na hipnose para tentar fazer com que espectadores deixem temporariamente em segundo plano as lembranças de um filme que já conhecem e possam assisti-lo novamente como se fosse a primeira vez.
articles.summary: O experimento Pathé Rewind utiliza hipnose no cinema para que espectadores deixem lembranças em segundo plano e redescubram clássicos com o impacto da primeira vez.
articles.body:
Cena da exibição do Filme "Divertidamente" durante o Festival de Cinema Acessível Kids — Foto: Foto: Gontof Comunicação/ Divulgação

Rede de cinemas na Holanda coloca em prática plano para hipnotizar espectadores. O objetivo: tentar fazê-los esquecer temporariamente filmes já vistos e recriar a sensação de assistir a uma história pela primeira vez. Que banda que já não existe você gostaria de ver ao vivo? Que personagem histórico teria vontade de conhecer? E se fosse possível reviver um daqueles momentos marcantes do cinema, como descobrir que Darth Vader é o pai de Luke Skywalker, se surpreender com a reviravolta de O Sexto Sentido ou assistir a Matrix sem fazer ideia do que é a Matrix?

É justamente essa experiência que a subsidiária holandesa da rede de cinemas Pathé quer testar.

Para recriar a sensação da primeira sessão, a empresa aposta na hipnose para tentar fazer com que espectadores deixem temporariamente em segundo plano as lembranças de um filme que já conhecem e possam assisti-lo novamente como se fosse a primeira vez.

Pathé Rewind: um experimento com hipnose

Nesta segunda-feira (9), até 30 participantes se reuniram no cinema Pathé Buitenhof, em Haia, para participar do experimento batizado de Pathé Rewind. A iniciativa conta com o hipnotizador Victor Kraemer, que, segundo a empresa, atua na área há mais de 30 anos.

Os voluntários se inscreveram previamente e, entre 30 de outubro e 8 de novembro, participaram de sessões individuais online com Kraemer. Pouco antes da exibição, eles passaram por uma nova sessão de hipnose na sala de cinema.

A proposta é tentar reduzir temporariamente a lembrança de um filme já assistido e verificar se os participantes conseguem recuperar parte da surpresa e do encantamento da primeira experiência.

Os inscritos puderam escolher entre quatro títulos: "Matrix", "Se7en", "Interestelar" e "La La Land". O filme exibido será aquele que recebeu o maior número de inscrições de pessoas dispostas a tentar "esquecê-lo" por algumas horas.

A iniciativa se encaixa em uma estratégia já conhecida da Pathé. Por meio do programa Pathé Classics, a rede costuma relançar filmes que marcaram gerações, como "Titanic" e , exibidos recentemente em uma mostra dedicada a Leonardo DiCaprio.

Segundo Imke van Schaaijk, diretora de marca, relações públicas e comunicação da empresa, muitos cinéfilos compartilham o desejo de redescobrir seus filmes favoritos. Com o Rewind, a Pathé pretende levar essa experiência um passo além.

A própria empresa ressalta que o objetivo não é comprovar a eficácia da hipnose, mas explorar se ela pode ajudar a recuperar a sensação de assistir a uma história pela primeira vez.

As regras do experimento também deixam claro que as sessões podem não produzir o efeito esperado e que a Pathé não se responsabiliza pelos resultados. A participação é voluntária e os inscritos podem interromper o processo a qualquer momento.

O projeto também desperta ceticismo. Críticos observam que a iniciativa tem um forte componente promocional e questionam se seus resultados poderão ser avaliados de forma objetiva, já que as conclusões dependerão, em grande parte, dos relatos dos próprios participantes.

Ainda assim, a proposta explora uma fantasia comum entre amantes do cinema: a possibilidade de apagar da memória, por algumas horas, uma história conhecida para voltar a experimentá-la com olhos de quem a vê pela primeira vez.

articles.title: Eneida Agra Maracajá recebe título de Doutora Honoris Causa da UEPB | G1
articles.standfirst: Solenidade de entrega da honraria acontece nesta terça-feira (10), no Teatro Municipal Severino Cabral, em Campina Grande. Professora é idealizadora do Festival de Inverno de Campina Grande, que completou 51 anos em 2026.
articles.summary: Solenidade de entrega da honraria acontece nesta terça-feira (10), no Teatro Municipal Severino Cabral, em Campina Grande. Professora é idealizadora do Festival de Inverno de Campina Grande, que completou 51 anos em 2026.
articles.body:
Eneida Agra Maracajá recebe título de Doutora Honoris Causa da UEPB — Foto: Ademar Trigueiro/TV Paraíba

A professora e ativista cultural Eneida Agra Maracajá recebeu, na noite desta terça-feira (10), o título de Doutora Honoris Causa da Universidade Estadual da Paraíba (UEPB). A solenidade aconteceu às 19h, no Teatro Municipal Severino Cabral, em Campina Grande . A homenagem reconhece mais de cinco décadas de trabalho dedicadas à educação e ao desenvolvimento das artes na Paraíba.

A concessão do título foi aprovada por unanimidade pelo Conselho Universitário (Consuni) da UEPB, em reunião realizada no dia 23 de setembro. A honraria é destinada a personalidades que se destacam pelo saber ou pela atuação nas artes, ciências, filosofia, letras e pelo entendimento entre os povos.

A trajetória de Eneida é marcada pela criação de iniciativas culturais e educativas que aproximam a arte da população. Entre os trabalhos estão o Festival de Inverno de Campina Grande (FICG) , o Tamanquinho das Artes e o Cultura no Presídio.

Em entrevista para a TV Paraíba , Eneida Maracajá ressaltou a felicidade com o reconhecimento e também relembrou que passou na UEPB como professora visitante na instituição por um longo período.

"Muita emoção, gratidão pelo reconhecimento a uma vida, uma história toda de compromisso, de dedicação, inclusive com a própria UEPB, que antes de ser UEPB, a Furne, cujo primeiro reitor foi Edvaldo do Ó, já tinha um profundo respeito e reconhecimento pelo nosso trabalho numa época em que eu ainda era professora da educação infantil", declarou.

Eneida Agra Maracajá é idealizadora do Festival de Inverno de Campina Grande (FICG), criado na década de 1970 e que completou 51 anos em 2026.

O festival surgiu a partir de um evento dedicado ao teatro, o Festival Nacional de Teatro (FENAT), realizado em 1974. Depois, passou a reunir diferentes manifestações artísticas, como teatro, dança, música, artes plásticas e literatura.

Em 2019, em entrevista ao g1 , Eneida relembrou a criação do festival e contou que, nos primeiros anos, artistas de diferentes estados chegaram a Campina Grande para participar das atividades. Segundo ela, o evento começou com apoio de recursos federais, estaduais e municipais, além de doações de moradores da cidade.

Eneida Agra Maracajá no Memorial Severino Cabral, sede do FICG, em Campina Grande — Foto: Yago Paolo/g1 PB

Além do FICG, Eneida criou projetos culturais voltados à população, como o Cultura no Presídio, realizado durante 13 anos no Complexo Penitenciário do Serrotão, e o Tamanquinhos das Artes, desenvolvido com crianças em situação de vulnerabilidade social.

Ela também foi diretora do Teatro Municipal Severino Cabral em duas gestões e secretária de Cultura de Campina Grande entre 2011 e 2012. É ainda fundadora do Instituto Solidarium, entidade responsável pelo desenvolvimento de projetos de caráter artístico, educativo e social.

Eneida é graduada em Pedagogia e tem mestrado em Educação. É professora efetiva da Universidade Federal da Paraíba (UFPB) e teve passagem pela própria UEPB e pela Faculdade Católica de Filosofia de Campina Grande.

Em 2025, a Pró-Reitoria de Cultura da UEPB articulou, junto à Assembleia Legislativa da Paraíba, o reconhecimento do Festival de Inverno como Patrimônio Imaterial da Cultura Paraibana.

Eneida Agra Maracajá é idealizadora do Festival de Inverno de Campina Grande (FICG), criado na década de 1970 e que completou 51 anos em 2026. — Foto: Divulgação/FICG

Em abril de 2026, Eneida lançou o livro "O Teatro na Educação Popular: diálogos entre Freire e Boal em uma experiência no bairro Mandacaru", publicado pela Editora da Universidade Estadual da Paraíba (EDUEPB) e pela editora A União.

A obra retoma a pesquisa de mestrado da professora, defendida em 1985, e apresenta uma experiência educativa realizada com moradores do bairro de Mandacaru, em João Pessoa . Na iniciativa, o teatro foi utilizado como ferramenta para abordar situações do cotidiano dos participantes.

articles.title: Papai Noel dos Correios 2026: como adotar cartinha em Juiz de Fora | G1
articles.standfirst: Cartinhas são escritas por estudantes de escolas públicas e crianças em situação de vulnerabilidade social. Interessados têm até o dia 8 de dezembro para escolher um pedido.
articles.summary: Papai Noel dos Correios 2026 em Juiz de Fora mobiliza padrinhos para atender pedidos de crianças carentes; escolha uma cartinha até 8 de dezembro e realize um sonho.
articles.body:
Correios na Marechal Deodoro em Juiz de Fora — Foto: Mariana Souza/g1

Começou nesta semana em Juiz de Fora a tradicional campanha 'Papai Noel dos Correios' . A ação, que consiste em adotar uma cartinha para presentear uma criança, está atualmente na fase de apadrinhamento.

As cartinhas são escritas por estudantes de escolas públicas , até o 5º ano do ensino fundamental, além de crianças em situação de vulnerabilidade social atendidas por instituições parceiras.

Os interessados têm até 8 de dezembro para acessar o site e escolher um ou mais pedidos que desejam atender. O presente deve ser entregue até o dia 10 do mesmo mês em uma das agências da cidade.

Rua Henrique Dias, n.º 187, no Bairro Benfica;

Avenida Presidente Itamar Franco, n.º 720, no Centro;

Avenida Rui Barbosa, n.º 474, no Bairro Santa Terezinha;

Rua Padre Café, n.º 138, no Bairro São Mateus;

Caso a pessoa prefira escolher a cartinha pessoalmente, basta ir à agência na Rua Marechal Deodoro, n.º 470, no Centro.

Além de Juiz de Fora, outras cidades da Zona da Mata e do Campo das Vertentes recebem a campanha.

Confira o endereço das agências nas cidades da região participantes:

Além Paraíba: seleção e entrega na Rua Coronel Oscar Cortes, n.º 91.

Barbacena: seleção e entrega na Rua José Bonifácio, n.º 23.

Carandaí: seleção e entrega na Praça Capitão Policarpo Rocha, n.º 46.

Carangola: seleção e entrega na Avenida Coronel Maximiano, n.º 36.

Muriaé: seleção e entrega na Praça Coronel Pacheco de Medeiros, n.º 260 e também na Rua Itagiba de Oliveira, n.º 16.

Cataguases: seleção e entrega na Avenida Astolfo Dutra, n.º 44.

São João del Rei: seleção e entrega na Avenida Tiradentes, n.º 500.

Santos Dumont: seleção e entrega na Rua Prefeito José Maria Pitella, n.º 33.

Ubá: seleção e entrega na Avenida Vereadora Rafael Girard, n.º 64.

Viçosa: seleção e entrega na Avenida Bueno Brandão, n.º 578; e na Praça Emílio Jardim, n.º 79.

A campanha surgiu em 1989, por iniciativa dos próprios funcionários. Eles recebiam cartinhas de crianças endereçadas ao Papai Noel ou destinadas ao Polo Norte, e começaram a comprar presentes para atender aos pedidos.

Com o aumento do número de cartas, os Correios abriram a campanha para toda a população em 1997. Desde então, qualquer pessoa pode adotar uma cartinha e presentear uma criança no Natal.

articles.title: Paul McCartney becomes the 7th musician to become a billionaire, joining the likes of Jay-Z, Taylor Swift, Rihanna, and more
articles.summary: Paul McCartney is now a billionaire, valued at $1.4 billion, joining the elite ranks of music's top earners like Jay-Z, Taylor Swift, and Rihanna. Discover the factors contributing to his wealth and his illustrious 69-year career in the music industry.
articles.body: Paul McCartney has made history after he was declared a billionaire, according to the latest reports shared online. The former Beatles member is now valued at USD 1.4 billion. McCartney has worked in the music industry for 69 years, from 1957 to the present, beginning his work with the Quarrymen and continuing through The Beatles, Wings, and his solo career. He is one of the most revered musicians in the industry.Paul McCartney becomes a billionaireAccording to Forbes, McCartney has officially joined the ranks of some of the most successful and most expensive musicians in the world. The report shared that the singer now has a net worth of USD 1.4 billion. The amount is thanks to the 84-year-old's musical catalogue, legal manoeuvres, tours, and art collection. According to the report, a lot of his funds also come from his own publishing company, which was founded in 1969. The label manages his own catalogue along with many other artists who have signed on.Some of the artists and songs under his label include Glenn Aitken, Buddy Holly, ‘It’s Beginning to Look a Lot Like Christmas,' ‘The Christmas Song (Chestnuts Roasting On An Open Fire),' ‘Blue Suede Shoes,' and many others. He also owns publishing rights to a large chunk of the Beatles discography. Other than this, McCartney also earns 25% of earnings from the Beatles’ holding company. The company generates about USD 50 million annually. The earnings come mainly from streaming residuals, vinyl sales, and merchandise.How many musicians have reached billionaire status?Over the years, six other artists in the industry, besides McCartney, have reached billionaire status. This includes Jay-Z with USD 2.8 billion, Taylor Swift with USD 2.0–2.1 billion, Rihanna with USD 1.4 billion, Bruce Springsteen with USD 1.2 billion, Beyoncé with USD 1.0–1.2 billion, and Dr. Dre with USD 1.0 billion.On the work front, McCartney’s latest album, 'The Boys of Dungeon Lane,' was released this past May. articles.title: Dustin Hoffman Denies Sexual Misconduct Allegations in New Memoir but Admits He May Have Made Women ‘Uncomfortable’
articles.summary: In his book ‘Look at Me,’ Hoffman makes reference to 2017’s #MeToo movement, likening it to McCarthyism
articles.body:
Dustin Hoffman opens up about serious allegations made against him in new memoir Look at Me

In the book, he denies allegations of sexual misconduct made against him amid 2017's #MeToo movement

"I'm sure it's true that in my life, especially forty years ago, I made some women uncomfortable," writes Hoffman, claiming that "'uncomfortable' is a subjective emotional state"

In his new memoir, Dustin Hoffman opens up about serious allegations that have been made against him over the years.

While Hoffman, 89, does not address specific accusations of sexual misconduct , which include claims from six different women that surfaced in 2017, Look at Me (on bookshelves Nov. 10) includes a chapter that delves into the actor's work in the controversial 1971 movie Straw Dogs and his 1982 hit Tootsie .

"I'm sure it's true that in my life, especially forty years ago, I made some women uncomfortable," writes the two-time Oscar winner. "But 'uncomfortable' is a subjective emotional state. What is crass and offensive to one person, another individual might find hilarious, or enlivening, or even sort of cozy."

Hoffman writes extensively about his sense of humor, calling himself "out there," in the memoir. "I love a so-called dirty joke. I am 'a Borscht Belt flirt,' as Bill Murray once put it. That's not the same thing as pressuring someone to do something they didn't want to do."

The father of six alludes to the #MeToo movement that began in 2017, writing, "When a reckoning started making its way around the internet, and tearing through Hollywood, I thought it was a very good thing. I knew by then that plenty of women had put up with way too much for way too long in my industry. Not for a second did I worry that anything negative would be said about me, because the idea of taking something from someone sexually that they didn't want to give... it's just not something I've ever done."

In 2017, three women spoke to Variety about their alleged encounters with Hoffman, accusing him of sexual harassment, sexual assault and exposing himself to a minor. While the actor issued a public apology to one accuser, his lawyer called the assault allegations from two of the women "defamatory falsehoods" at the time.

Earlier that year, three women separately accused Hoffman of sexual harassment, with one claiming she was assaulted when she was 17 years old as a production assistant on Death of a Salesman in 1985, the same production on which a second woman said Hoffman groped and assaulted her. A third woman claimed Hoffman propositioned her during a pitch meeting. No lawsuits or criminal charges were brought against Hoffman.

Likening the allegations of sexual misconduct against men in power to the McCarthy era of the early 1950s, in which Hollywood figures and other notable Americans were blacklisted for affiliations with communism, Hoffman writes his "entire life changed" amid the reckoning. "There was no innocent until proven guilty. There was no 'proving' anything at all."

He continues, "The whole thing was so crazy, I was sort of bewildered by how to defend myself... or if I should even try. I didn't want to be fighting against something that I thought was important. I didn't want to be on the wrong side of my own values. The only problem was that things were being said about me that just weren't true."

In Look at Me , Hoffman writes that he has "learned a lot from" Lisa , his wife since 1980, "about men and women and the different ways we perceive a given situation. It took me years (decades?) to understand that flirting with every woman I met was not okay."

He continues, "It's not that Lisa has ever doubted my love or my commitment. (Many times over the years, she has noticed me staring at a pretty woman, and said, 'Dusty, would you like me to introduce you?') She knows who she's dealing with. She fell in love with a guy with a bawdy sense of humor who is obsessed with sex and is always looking for attention."

He adds that it took "an embarrassingly long time to grasp that if I was flirting or my jokes were too dirty, people who were not my wife might think I was being inappropriate. I know I'm harmless, she knows I'm harmless, but if you'd never met me before, would you know? ... I'm not looking to humiliate or offend anybody. I'm not a person who gets off on having power, or pressuring people to do things. To be perfectly honest, I never thought of myself as a person with power in the first place."

The Rain Man star also writes, "Is it possible that I've been guilty of insufficient empathy? That I was too self-involved to correctly perceive what the people around me were feeling all the time? Sure. Of course."

He concludes the chapter, "If you don't feel the same way, then you are different from every other human being I've met in this life. Male or female."

Hoffman most recently appeared on the big screen in the movies Tuner and Diamond . His memoir Look at Me will be available wherever books are sold on Nov. 10.

articles.title: ‘Get Huge’: The dark side of looksmaxxing and the deaths that shocked many
articles.summary: A new documentary, "Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death," explores the dark world of looksmaxxing and the deaths that shocked the manosphere.
articles.body:
The online creator "Elon Muscular" was 15, living with five people in a one-bedroom apartment in South Brooklyn, and feeling like he'd reached his breaking point.

He was suicidal and felt like no one was listening .

A Google search for "how to cure depression" first introduced him to the world of biohacking, a DIY approach to maximizing physical health and longevity that set the precedent for the rise of the "looksmaxxing" side of the internet.

The influencer Clavicular — who has gone to extremes such as hitting himself in the face with a hammer so his bones supposedly grow back sharper and taking small amounts of methamphetamine in an attempt to suppress his appetite — brought looksmaxxing to the mainstream zeitgeist. But before him, before Andrew Tate brought the manosphere into focus, and before Bryan Johnson became synonymous with modern biohacking tips, there was Anthony Hughes.

Known by the persona "Tony Huge," the lawyer-turned-buff-bodybuilder amassed hundreds of thousands of followers on his YouTube channel for videos about using psychedelics, steroids, and other substances to reach what he deemed to be peak male performance — that included the use of illegal chemicals in extreme amounts.

That world, and the loneliness that draws young men to it, is at the center of " Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death ," a three-part docuseries premiering on Hulu on Nov. 10.

Muscular, identified only by his online moniker in the docuseries, recalled how he was entranced by Hughes, who lived by the mantra, "a day natty [natural] is a day wasted." Hughes had Ferraris, a mansion, and videos with bikini-clad women. It seemed like he knew something about life that Muscular didn't.

"It made me feel like I wasn't alone," Muscular said.

The series follows Hughes and the community of extreme biohackers around him, who experimented with illegal drugs, steroids, peptides, and risky body-modification techniques in pursuit of bigger muscles, bigger penises, improved sexual performance, and eternal youth. It also investigates a series of deaths among those in Hughes' inner circle, some of which remain unsolved, while charting how his brand of self-optimization at any cost helped lay the groundwork for today's looksmaxxing movement.

"When this series began, looksmaxxing wasn't even in the cultural conversation at that point," director Stacey Lee told USA TODAY. "I really felt it was important to tell a story that humanizes this very complex situation."

The scene of the story is Hughes' compound in Pattaya, Thailand. Muscular was 19 when he received an invite to join Hughes there after messaging the influencer on Facebook.

There, he interacted with close friends of Hughes, like Leo and Longevity, whose real name is Laith Abdallah Algaz, a fellow biohacker and penis-enlargement advocate who died mysteriously in January 2023 in the bathroom of their shared compound. Local police found Algaz dead from blunt-force head trauma, but the case is still unsolved.

Many of the young men initially drawn to this space were seeking community and spaces to ask questions openly, while improving their physical, economic, and romantic circumstances.

"So many of the young men that are drawn to this are using looksmaxxing as a means of solving what is incredibly complex societal issues, and I think therein lies some of the challenges," Lee said. "The need to make your muscles bigger, or your jawline a certain way, or your brow line a certain way, or your penis bigger, all of these things are superficial aspects of the self."

Much of the series explores the questions swirling around the deaths in Hughes' inner orbit, which, besides Leo and Longevity, also included looksmaxxers Nick Weisser in 2018 and Josh Brooks in 2021. The deaths quickly fueled accusations, finger-pointing, and conspiracy theories, driving a wedge among the men who were part of this tight-knit community.

The series also features Connor Murphy, a looksmaxxing internet creator combining performance art, pick up lines, pranks and fitness who also spent time at Hughes' Thailand compound. Four weeks after filming concluded, Murphy died at age 32 after drowning in a lake in Thailand.

"His passing kind of reinforced our responsibility to show that complicated, multi-dimensional side of him beyond just the online performance… that you know was I think in some ways misunderstood on the internet," Lee said.

'Young boys are looking at this content and thinking about it like a blueprint for their own life'

Lee grew interested in looksmaxxing after the 2024 presidential election, when she saw young men gravitate toward male lifestyle creators who merged fitness, politics and culture. President Donald Trump appeared on shows from creators like the Nelk Boys , Theo Von , Joe Rogan and Adin Ross , helping sway Gen Z men his way in a phenomenon some have since deemed the " bro " vote.

"These kind of masculine role models are emerging in the online sphere, and we're witnessing a lot of young males take upon these mantras," Lee said.

Lee pointed out that, as influencers, much of these creators' content was manufactured for clicks, likes, and engagement. But it's hard for young viewers to discern the difference between performance and sound advice.

"I wanted to find what was real," Lee said. "If young boys are looking at this content and thinking about it like a blueprint for their own life, then what aspects of this are genuine aspects of masculinity?"

"So much of this world, so much of what they're doing, is performance," she added.

The combination of technology and the natural insecurities that arise during teenage years creates a "perfect storm" for innocuous sports and health spaces to tune young men into radical content, Gary Barker, the president of Equimundo: Center for Masculinities and Social Justice, an organization that advocates for healthy manhood , previously told USA TODAY.

"You see with the story of [Muscular], as we follow him down that path, he's trying to cure depression… and what he finds is community, he finds belonging," Lee said. "He finds people that make him believe that he can become the best version of himself."

Lee, a mother to a 9-year-old-son and 6-year-old-daughter, hopes that adding context and nuance to the conversation around masculinity, and teaching her kids discernment about how much of what they watch online is performed, will teach them critical thinking around gender ideology.

"When the kids get nightmares or bad dreams, you turn on the lights. You help them show that the boogeyman's not so scary," Lee said, explaining that a large part of the project was leaning into discomfort rather than turning away from it. "I think the boogeyman is scarier when you don't understand it."

articles.title: Attack on Titan 3 confirms a major change that puts Eren Yeager's legacy in a new light
articles.summary: Eren Yeager may have been the face of Attack on Titan for years, but the upcoming third game is giving fans a chance to experience the brutal world of
articles.body: Eren Yeager may have been the face of Attack on Titan for years, but the upcoming third game is giving fans a chance to experience the brutal world of Titans through a completely different set of eyes. Koei Tecmo is introducing a customisable Scout who will take centre stage in the new adventure. The change does not erase Eren's legacy. Instead, it gives players a personal role in one of anime's most emotionally charged stories, with familiar characters, dangerous missions and a fresh character-driven ending.Attack on Titan 3 lets players create their own heroThe biggest change in Attack on Titan 3 is the introduction of a player-created protagonist. Rather than controlling the entire experience through Eren's perspective, players can design their own Scout and become part of the Survey Corps.The customisation options offer plenty of room for creativity. Players can adjust facial features, hairstyles, body types and outfits. They can also add smaller details, including glasses and chokers, to give their characters a distinct appearance.However, the new hero will not be fighting alone. The character will join familiar faces such as Mikasa Ackerman, Armin Arlert and Levi. Players can also build relationships with other members of the regiment at headquarters, with these connections affecting squad performance during missions.Combat is also receiving attention. The developers have refined the omni-directional mobility gear, allowing players to move through Titan-infested areas with greater control. Special Exterior Missions will add another layer of strategy, putting players in charge of squad decisions, supply bases and battlefield retreats.The game is scheduled to arrive on December 10, 2026, for PC, PlayStation 5, Nintendo Switch 2 and Xbox Series X|S.Attack on Titan 3 promises a different ending for its new protagonistThe new character also brings an interesting narrative change. According to producer Hideo Suzuki, the game will cover the complete story, from the fall of Wall Maria to the events of the fourth season. However, players will experience those events through their own Scout.In an interview with Crunchyroll published on October 30, Suzuki explained why the team chose this approach.“So in the previous game, the story hadn’t ended. To conclude our game, we had to come up with some kind of ending to it, and therefore, we had this “what-if” scenario... For this game, since we’re covering the entire story, there’s already an ending to it. So it wouldn’t make sense to have our own ending to the story in a game. Because this story would be told from the perspective of your main character, it’s not like a “what-if” type of ending. But there is an ending for your particular character.”This means Eren's established fate will remain intact, while the custom Scout will receive a separate conclusion to their personal journey.For longtime fans, this could make familiar events feel different without changing the original story. Players will know how the larger conflict ends, but their own character will have a story worth experiencing.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: ‘Yellowstone’ star Dawn Olivieri chose Arkansas ranch life over LA to reclaim her ‘freedom’
articles.summary: "Yellowstone" star Dawn Olivieri reveals the career dry spell that drove her to leave LA for a 160-acre Arkansas ranch and animal sanctuary.
articles.body: "Yellowstone" alum Dawn Olivieri is opening up about the turning point that drove her to leave Los Angeles behind and build the life that she actually wanted on a ranch and animal sanctuary in rural Arkansas. During an interview with Fox News Digital, the 45-year-old actress, who is starring in the second season of Angel Studios’ post-apocalyptic drama "Homestead: The Series," shared how she became disillusioned with Hollywood during a lull in her career after years of chasing acting success. "I realized it wasn't giving me what my dream of what it was supposed to give me," Olivieri said. 'VAMPIRE DIARIES' STAR IAN SOMERHALDER SAYS LEAVING HOLLYWOOD FOR FARMING 'SHIFTED MY LIFE FOREVER' "It wasn't cooperating," she continued. "I didn't have offers, just like falling out of my phone. I went through a dry spell, and I was like, ‘Wow, so this is an illusion.'" "I kind of saw through the veil and once I saw through veil — I realized in that moment, I have to make some decisions about my life that makes me happy — [it] isn't always waiting by the phone, losing my power, waiting for someone to hire me," Olivieri recalled. "I'm like, ‘Oh, what am I doing?’" 'HOMESTEAD' STAR BAILEY CHASE SAYS CALIFORNIA VACCINE PLANS WERE 'FINAL STRAW' THAT DROVE FAMILY OUT OF LA "I just jumped ahead," she explained. "I go, ‘If I did make all this money and was successful, what would I do with it?’ Well, I would move to the country and have horses and OK, well, I guess let me go do that. Let me, let me see what. And so I did that with nothing. Which wasn't the dream part, but in actuality, it was what was always meant to happen because I moved toward my own authenticity." In 2022, the actress left LA and bought a 160-acre property outside Mena, Arkansas. The following year, Olivieri founded the nonprofit organization Moon Mountain Sanctuary and Rescue, which rescues and rehabilitates hundreds of horses and other animals. 'LIONESS' STAR JILL WAGNER RAISES DAUGHTERS IN TENNESSEE TOWN OF 800, WHERE HORSES AND BUGGIES STILL ROAM During an August appearance on the "Let's Talk Local" podcast, Olivieri said she is currently living in a camper on the property while she continues to build and expand her ranch and animal sanctuary. While speaking with Fox News Digital, Olivieri reflected on the unexpected result that came from her decision to leave Hollywood and create the lifestyle she had always envisioned, explaining that giving up control of her acting career ultimately improved it. HOLLYWOOD STAR SOUNDS ALARM OVER DISAPPEARING JOBS AS PRODUCTIONS FLEE CALIFORNIA "I think in that moment, I became a better human being," she said. "I became a better actress for sure. I started working way more than I did when I was in LA waiting for the job, waiting for the call." "And I moved to a land of no mirrors is what I called it," Olivieri continued.. "I went into a deep relationship with the core of my being versus what everything looked like, what I looked like." "And I would recommend that move to anybody," she added. Olivieri's "Homestead: The Series" co-star Charles Esten, who joined her for the interview, agreed that letting go of the pressure to land the next role can sometimes have the opposite effect in Hollywood. "It’s not just Hollywood, it’s the whole world that — but especially Hollywood — can smell that desperation of, ‘I need this to get that,’" Esten said. WATCH: ‘YELLOWSTONE’ STAR DAWN OLIVIERI TRADED LA FOR ARKANSAS RANCH "The second you sort of don’t hold so tightly and you have sort of more philosophy of abundance and let it a little looser. Or another way is just give it up," he continued. "I don’t mean give it up by quit doing it, but give up the need and the desperation on it. And then they finally go, ‘Hey, you want to come do a show?’" "Yeah, literally, that’s what happened," Olivieri replied. Olivieri pointed out that many other actors faced a dramatic decrease in work opportunities in recent years due to the COVID-19 pandemic and the 2023 SAG-AFTRA and the Writers Guild of America (WGA) strike. 'VERONICA MARS' STAR JASON DOHRING TRADED HOLLYWOOD FOR FARMING "But I had a very clear decision that I was willing to give up this identity of being an actress," she said. "And maybe if I had to sell farm fresh eggs on the side of the road, I would do that just to keep my freedom." "Homestead: The Series" follows survivors living at a fortified prepper compound in the Rocky Mountains known as The Homestead after a nuclear attack on LA plunges the country into chaos. Olivieri plays Jenna Ross, the wife of Ian Ross (Neal McDonough), the wealthy prepper who established the Homestead, while Esten portrays Cain Ross, Ian's estranged brother. After Ian is incapacitated and later dies, Jenna is pushed into a leadership role and struggles with how to protect the community while maintaining her compassionate approach toward outsiders. Meanwhile, Cain arrives at the Homestead after Ian's injury and takes a much more hardline approach to survival and leadership. In season two, which premiered on Nov. 3, Jenna and Cain find themselves in conflict over how the compound should be run as resources dwindle. Olivieri was part of the cast in the 2024 theatrical movie "Homestead," which introduces the story. Esten joined the cast for the first season of "Homestead: The Series," which picks up where the movie left off. The show also stars Kevin Lawson Emmanuel McCord, Jesse Hutch and Betzaida Landín. While speaking with Fox News Digital, Olivieri and Esten shared their thoughts on why more Americans are increasingly interested in homesteading, growing their own food and moving away from big cities. "People are thinking about it because everything else is becoming toxic in all truth," Olivieri said. "Our food system has gone toxic because of profit. Our way of life in a city has become toxic because of overpopulation potentially or, again, I really think the root of it is profit and money and commerce." "In this state of government, being open and available is just a nicer experience," she added. "It is for me anyway." Esten drew a contrast between Olivieri's homesteading and the gritty survivalism depicted on "Homestead: The Series." "Dawn's homesteading that I've noticed is beautiful," he said. "Our version of homestead is very extraordinary necessity, fear-based. Plant these fences and Dawn's is the opposite of that. Dawn's very open and welcoming and saving animals that need it and welcoming other folks on." After Olivieri embraced rural life and stopped waiting for Hollywood to call, the actress went on to land major roles in Taylor Sheridan's universe. Olivieri played Claire Dutton, the widowed sister of James Dutton (Tim McGraw), in 2021's "1883." From 2022 to 2024, Olivieri portrayed Sarah Atwood, the corporate strategist brought in by Market Equities who becomes involved with Jamie Dutton (Wes Bentley), in "Yellowstone." She has a recurring role as CIA officer Amber Whalen on "Lioness" and most recently made a guest appearance in "The Madison." While speaking with Fox News Digital, Olivieri weighed in on what she believes sets the prolific creator apart from others in Hollywood. "He doesn't ask for permission to do anything," she said. "He listens to his North, his guide, and he writes textured, powerful human beings, especially women, which I find is very, very rare." "I've talked to him about this because he will write things for a strong woman that makes you read it on the page and then look around, like, ‘Is someone watching me? How are you in my head?’" Olivieri recalled asking Sheridan how he was able to write female characters with such insight. "I went to him and I said, ‘How do you know how to do that?’ And he told me point blank, he said his mom was a strong woman," she remembered. "So he had a very, very, very close example of how strong women move and what they do and how they think and the way that they talk." LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS "He writes things poetically," she continued. "He has texture. There's magic in the way that he writes and it's just undeniable. And he agrees he's tapped. He'll sit and wait for the muse and the muse will share the story with him. And that's how he writes." "They are a conduit for some energy that flows through them. And he has told me that that's exactly what happens for him." articles.title: Russell Brand, Katy Perry video resurfaces, sparking concern after conviction
articles.summary: Russell Brand held up an "obey" sign as Katy Perry spoke to a reporter, with the 2010 clip resurfacing and sparking concern after his rape conviction.
articles.body:
A red carpet interview with former couple Katy Perry and Russell Brand is resurfacing, and some viewers are looking at Brand's behavior through a new lens.

The red-carpet exchange is drawing fresh scrutiny after a London jury convicted Brand of rape and sexual assault ⁠ Nov. 5. A judge sentenced the British comedian, 51, to 10 years and six months in prison ⁠ Tuesday, Nov. 9.

The 2010 video shows a reporter asking Perry which Academy Award winners she was happiest for following the awards show, at Vanity Fair's annual Oscar party March 7 outside the Sunset Tower Hotel in West Hollywood, California⁠.

Perry and Brand stopped to talk to British morning show "GMTV," and when Brand starts to give his take on the Academy Awards, Perry laughs.

Brand tries to answer the question himself and holds up a small tag that read "obey." "You didn't watch it!" she said. Brand insists he had. When Perry uses an expletive (as seen in the video below), he tells her, "don't swear."

After Brand holds up the tag, the reporter turns back to Perry and asks how she dealt with him. "He's actually hilarious," Perry replied. "He leaves me speechless."

Photographs from that night⁠ shows Brand also holding the tag toward the cameras as he posed beside Perry. A logo resembling artist Shepard Fairey's Obey logo appears next to the word.

The video has sparked a larger conversation online, with one X user (@Xx17965797N) describing Brand as using the tag "to control her." Some viewers who revisited the footage after the verdict called the exchange "disturbing" in the comment section.

"Mind you he used to use an 'obey' tag on katy perry every time she wasn't agreeing with him," wrote @notwhomstfarted. "imagine the horrors he did behind closed doors…"

USA TODAY reached out to Perry's representatives for comment.

Six women accused Brand of sexual offenses dating from 1999 to 2009. At his 2026 trial in London, jurors convicted him of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault and acquitted him of the three remaining charges. He has denied the allegations against him.

What Katy Perry said about her marriage to Russell Brand

Perry and Brand married in India in October 2010⁠. In a 2013 interview with Vogue ⁠, Perry said she often invited him to join her on the road and tried to get home when she could.

"He didn't like the atmosphere of me being the boss on tour." Perry said. "So that was really hurtful, and it was very controlling, which was upsetting."

Fourteen months after their wedding, Brand sent her a text on New Year's Eve 2011 saying he wanted a divorce, Perry told Vogue. At the time of the interview, she said, it was the last she'd heard from him.

The Crown Prosecution Service ⁠ said Brand committed sex crimes against four women between 2004 and 2009, before he married Perry. Prosecutors agreed to leave the marriage out of their opening statement after his lawyers objected. Brand later told jurors that marrying Perry had brought him "staggering fame."

Contributing: Liza Esquibias, Brendan Morrow, USA TODAY

articles.body: Country music legend Dolly Parton’s initiative to encourage children to read has reached an extraordinary milestone, with her Imagination Library having gifted more than 300 million free books to children since its launch in 1995. Adding to the celebration, the Country Music Association (CMA), Belmont University, The Walt Disney Company and the Nashville Convention & Visitors Corp (NCVC) have come together to contribute a combined $1 million towards the programme.The announcement followed the star-studded television special, CMA Presents I Will Always Love You: A Celebration of Dolly Parton, which honoured the singer's remarkable musical journey and her contribution to generations of fans. While the evening celebrated her legacy as a performer and songwriter, the donation highlighted another side of Parton's life: her commitment to childhood literacy and education.Dolly Parton launched the Imagination Library in 1995 inspired by her fatherThe story behind the Imagination Library is deeply personal. Parton was inspired to start the initiative by her father, who was unable to read or write. Wanting to ensure that children had access to books from an early age, she launched the programme in her home county of Sevier, Tennessee, in 1995.What began as a local initiative soon grew into an international book-gifting programme. Its central idea remains simple: give young children access to books and encourage them to develop a love for reading before they begin school.Today, the Imagination Library operates across the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia and the Republic of Ireland. It has gifted more than 300 million books since its inception and mails over three million age-appropriate books to children every month.Under the programme, every enrolled child receives one book every month from birth until the age of five, completely free of cost to their families.Disney, CMA and partners contribute $1 million to Dolly Parton's initiativeThe latest $1 million contribution brings together four organisations that joined hands to celebrate Parton's legacy. The Country Music Association, Belmont University, The Walt Disney Company and Nashville Convention & Visitors Corp collectively announced the donation following the television tribute.CMA CEO Sarah Trahern said the event was designed to bring people together, much like Parton's music has done over the years. She highlighted how the performances and support from partners had helped turn a celebration of the singer into a meaningful contribution towards children's literacy.CMA incoming CEO Brittany Schaffer also acknowledged Parton's influence through her music, philanthropy and generosity, adding that the initiative would help carry her legacy forward for future generations.Belmont University President Dr Greg Jones said that a love of learning could open doors and shape the future of young people. He expressed gratitude for the opportunity to celebrate Parton's life while helping put more books into children's hands.Nashville Convention & Visitors Corp President and CEO Deana Ivey also spoke about the singer's connection with the city, describing her as one of Music City's greatest ambassadors. She said the organisation was proud to support a cause that remained close to Parton's heart.Jeff Conyers, President and Vice Chair of The Dollywood Foundation, said the donation was a meaningful way to celebrate Parton's life by investing in the dreams of future generations.A star-studded musical tribute celebrates Dolly Parton's legacyThe fundraising announcement followed CMA Presents I Will Always Love You: A Celebration of Dolly Parton, a special featuring several prominent country music artists performing some of her most memorable songs.The performances included Ella Langley singing Jolene, Kelsea Ballerini performing Here You Come Again, Ashley McBryde taking on Coat of Many Colors and Darius Rucker performing Two Doors Down.Other highlights included Lady A performing Islands in the Stream, Carly Pearce and Kristin Chenoweth joining forces for 9 to 5, and Little Big Town performing Light of a Clear Blue Morning.Carrie Underwood led the full cast in a performance of I Will Always Love You, while Zac Brown presented Butterfly in a vocal duet with Dolly Parton.The television special is now available to stream on Disney+ and Hulu.How Dolly Parton's book programme continues to reach millions of childrenThe Imagination Library is the flagship initiative of The Dollywood Foundation, a non-profit organisation that works with thousands of local programme partners to make the book-gifting model possible.While the foundation manages the partnerships, resources and systems behind the initiative, local partners help create awareness and raise funds to cover the wholesale cost of books and their delivery.This collaborative model has allowed Parton's original dream to reach millions of households across different countries. More than three million books are now mailed every month, giving children an opportunity to build their own home libraries from an early age.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: Anupam Kher 'completely overwhelmed' by Sweden's response to 'Ramayana: Rise of a Legend'; says, 'People came up to me with tears in their eyes' after Stockholm premiere
articles.summary: Veteran actor Anupam Kher has shared glimpses from the Stockholm premiere of Nitesh Tiwari’s ‘Ramayana: Rise of a Legend’, saying the warm reaction of
articles.body: Veteran actor Anupam Kher has shared glimpses from the Stockholm premiere of Nitesh Tiwari’s ‘Ramayana: Rise of a Legend’, saying the warm reaction of Swedish viewers left him overwhelmed. Anupam Kher, who voices Jatayu in the film, posted a video showing audience members shaking hands and chatting with him after the screening.Anupam Kher’s note on the Stockholm premiere‘Ramayana’ reached theatres on 5 November, just in time for Diwali. It had premieres across the world and got mixed reviews from critics, but it has done well at the box office.Anupam Kher wrote a long note on X and Instagram about the Sweden event. “Extremely happy to share these visuals from the Swedish premiere of Ramayana: The Rise of Legend in Stockholm. I began my speech with a sentence in Swedish: “Jag är mycket glad att vara här i Stockholm i kväll.” — “I am very happy to be here in Stockholm this evening.” And I truly was. After 41 years and 556 films in India, it was also special to share that I have become a small part of Swedish cinema for the first time with Out of Fashion,” he wrote.Anupam Kher's message of the epic travels across bordersThanking Anurag Bhushan, India’s Ambassador to Sweden, for the introduction, Anupam Kher said he felt proud to be part of the film by voicing Jatayu. “The Ramayana is not only a story from India; its message of love, sacrifice, family, duty and the triumph of good over evil speaks to people across borders, languages and generations. It was moving to see this timeless Indian epic being celebrated in Sweden,” he wrote.Audience left the actor emotionalAnupam Kher said the response after the film moved him deeply. “When the film ended, people came up to me with tears in their eyes, shaking my hand and thanking me for telling the story of the Ramayana and for playing Jatayu. I was completely overwhelmed. It filled me with immense pride to see a film like this come out of India and connect with audiences here,” he wrote.He congratulated the film’s team and ended his note with, “Proud to be Indian. Jai Shri Ram!”About ‘Ramayana: Rise of a Legend’The film stars Ranbir Kapoor as Rama, Sai Pallavi as Sita and Yash as Ravana. Nitesh Tiwari has directed it, and Namit Malhotra and Yash have produced it on a very large budget. The first part covers Rama’s birth, upbringing, marriage and vanavas. It closes with Ravana abducting Sita and Rama vowing to defeat him. The second part is set to release for Diwali 2028.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: Toukie Smith, ‘227’ actor and Robert De Niro’s former partner, dies at 74
articles.summary: Toukie Smith, a model, actor and mother of twins with ex-partner Robert De Niro, died at 74, her children announced.
articles.body: Toukie Smith, a model, actor and mother of twins with ex-partner Robert De Niro, died at 74, her children announced. The former “227” sitcom actor died on Nov. 4 after “a long, courageous battle with multiple sclerosis,” according to a statement released by her children, Airyn and Julian, whom she shared with De Niro. Smith was also the sister of legendary fashion designer Willi Smith, who died at 39 in 1987 from complications from AIDS. Toukie Smith also modeled for him, as well as for other luminaries like Hubert de Givenchy and Patrick Kelly. “As the sister of the late, legendary designer Willi Smith, Toukie shared in a remarkable family legacy that helped shape American fashion and culture,” her children wrote. “She was a model, muse and collaborator, not only to her beloved brother but to other trailblazing luminaries of the era, including the illustrator Alvaro, Jean-Paul Goude, Patrick Kelly and Antonio Lopez,” the statement continues. “Her beauty, grace and unmistakable presence helped pave the way for generations of Black models and designers in fashion.” Smith also played artist Eva Rawley on the hit NBC sitcom “227” starring Marla Gibbs, which ran from 1985 to 1990. She also appeared in multiple episodes of the classic ‘80s show “Miami Vice.” She and De Niro were partners from 1988 to 1996, according to The Hollywood Reporter. Airyn and Julian were conceived by in vitro fertilization and delivered by a surrogate mother. De Niro has five additional children with three other women. “Toukie was a force of nature,” her children wrote. “She left an indelible mark on our hearts and on everyone lucky enough to know her.” What Was Toukie Smith’s Cause of Death? The actor and model died following a “long” battle with multiple sclerosis, according to a statement by her two children. It’s not clear how long she had the autoimmune condition, but her children said in their statement that she died after a “long, courageous battle.” Toukie Smith and Robert De Niro at a benefit honoring Willi Smith.Ron Galella / Ron Galella Collection via Getty What Is Multiple Sclerosis? Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune condition that affects your central nervous system due to your immune system mistakenly attacking the protective sheaths that surround the nerves in your brain and spinal cord, according to Cleveland Clinic. There are almost a million adults in the United States living with the condition, per the Cleveland Clinic. Symptoms of MS include the following: Double vision or vision lossMuscle weaknessNumbness or abnormal sensationsFatigueLoss of balance or coordinationMuscle stiffness and spasmsDifficulty with memory, concentration, learning and judgmentMood changesDizzinessDifficulty regulating bladder There isn’t a single tool to diagnose someone with MS, which can sometimes make detecting it difficult for doctors. “It can take time before you receive an official MS diagnosis,” according to the Cleveland Clinic. “You may need to make several trips to see your provider before you know for sure. This happens because MS symptoms can look like or happen with several other common conditions.” While there is no cure for multiple sclerosis, there are treatments available to minimize symptoms and flare-ups. Still, MS can lead to disability, especially over time, and can be fatal in rare cases, according tot he Cleveland Clinic.

articles.title: Jon Stewart on Trump’s testy 60 Minutes interview: ‘Was that sass?’
articles.summary: Late-night hosts discussed Trump’s interview with the ‘new, Maga-fied’ CBS program and Stephen Miller’s White House promotion
articles.body:
Late-night hosts reacted to Donald Trump 's strange interview with 60 Minutes and his unpopular promotion of Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff.

A week after Democrats' decisive victories in the US midterm elections , widely seen as a repudiation of Trump, Jon Stewart checked in with the beleaguered president. "Donald Trump headed over to the newly Maga-fied CBS for a little self-soothing with one of 60 Minutes's new correspondents, a religious conservative by the name of Ross Douthat," he said on Monday's Daily Show.

On the once-storied news program, Trump claimed that "we have created wealth at a level that our country has never seen before" – "including for yourself," Douthat cut in.

"Young man, was that sass?" Stewart laughed. "Did the new Maga-fied CBS 60 Minutes just deliver sass to Donald Trump? I think you're supposed to 'yes, and … ' not 'yes, but … '."

Trump tried to defend himself, claiming that "everyone's" wealth increased, but Douthat again countered: "My net worth did not go up by $3bn."

"I think I'm going to enjoy this," Stewart relished. "I did not come into this interview thinking: 'Uh, I'm going to enjoy this.' But now, as I am watching this, I am thinking to myself: 'I am going to enjoy this.' Let me prepare the table for the feast we are all about to enjoy. As regular viewers of our program know, Donald Trump has a somewhat high regard for his own financial acumen. In fact, not 20 minutes prior, in this very same interview we are watching, Donald Trump said this: 'I'm really good at money and finances.'"

And yet in the same interview, Trump said of his own fortune: "I guess it's gone up. I don't even know."

"My frustration with reporters is, I wish someone would, like, hammer down on this," said Stewart. "Trump acts like he's got all this money squirreled away in some index fund, and it just magically grew. Meanwhile, since the guy has returned to office, he's made $125m from foreign golf and real-estate schemes, $117m from legal settlements, $636m from selling that bullshit novelty meme coin. He's gotten $800m from his World Liberty Financial crypto company. Why can't someone just bring this up to his face?"

Douthat did, in fact, ask Trump about World Liberty Financial, which is partly owned by investors connected to the government of the United Arab Emirates. "I think if I told you that story," he said, "and it was about the Biden family, if I said Joe Biden is the part-owner of a company and it has all of these investments from the Middle East, you would say that sounds corrupt."

"I'll have what he's having," Stewart cheered, referencing the famous scene from When Harry Met Sally. "I love that Douthat is forcing Trump to compare himself to the Biden crime family."

In response to that comparison, Trump claimed the difference was he knew "nothing about" his son's business.

"My god, Ross, you beautiful bearded bastard," Stewart cheered. "Do you know what you've just done here? Do you have any idea what you just did here? You have made Donald Trump admit that the difference between him and Joe Biden is that Joe Biden is more aware of his surroundings."

On Jimmy Kimmel Live!, the host kept track of Trump's reaction to the midterms landslide, which quickly morphed from accepting the results to questioning the legitimacy of the results. Over the weekend, Trump posted on Truth Social: "Does anybody really believe that this 'Election' was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong???"

"This is how it starts," Kimmel said. "This is how he does a little taste of conspiracy. Nothing too intense, just enough to whet your appetite. And then he feeds it a little more. It grows. The lie gets bigger. He keeps repeating it.

"And then he starts talking about people talking about him claiming the election was rigged, as if there are people other than him claiming the election was rigged,. And before you know it, someone in a Viking helmet is making a toilet out of Nancy Pelosi's desk. God bless America!"

"I don't think we're prepared for the amount of insanity that this drama queen president is about to pump on us," Kimmel added. "Donald Trump right now is a raccoon in a duffel bag. He's been cut off at the cankles. And there are two possible paths he can take. The first one is to check out. No more meetings. Lots of trips to Mar-a-Lago. Lots of golf with Natalie running behind the cart. Every once in a while he'll host a Super Bowl team. That's the best case scenario."

But the host also saw a different, much darker future on the horizon. "Scenario number two is he goes nuts. Like Jack Nicholson in The Shining nuts. Everybody who works for him gets the axe. He turns on anybody who might possibly want to succeed him, whether that be Lil Marco or JD Vance. Even his own son. Even if Don Jr decides to run for president, his father will say and do anything he can to destroy him. Because he wants to make sure no one but him will ever live in the White House again. He might knock down the rest of it for all we know."

And on Late Night, Seth Meyers post-gamed the midterms. "The GOP is furious with Trump and blaming him for their historic drubbing, which might be why Trump is suddenly pretending to strike a more conciliatory tone," he noted.

In that 60 Minutes interview, Douthat asked Trump: "If it took six months of not insulting the Democrats to get a deal done, do you think you could do it?" Trump, who had just called the Democrats "dumb-ocrats," answered: "Very easily."

"Very easily?!" Meyers marveled. "You couldn't even get through the question without insulting Democrats. He's like a guilty dog who also offers up more things he did."

But despite his gesturing at conciliation, Trump this weekend promoted Stephen Miller, the hardline architect of the president's unpopular immigration crackdown, to be the new White House chief of staff. "It's especially absurd that Trump would promote the most unhinged member of his staff, given that he also specifically cited immigration as an area where he could like to compromise with Democrats," Meyers said.

In the 60 Minutes interview, Trump conceded that his hardline immigration policy "might be too tough".

"Stephen Miller is the guy who created that policy!" Meyers exclaimed. "Why are you promoting the guy responsible for the thing you admit people hate! It's like if Subway made Jared Fogle their CEO."

"How can Trump say that he wants to work with Democrats on immigration while promoting Stephen Miller at the same time?" he concluded. "It may seem contradictory, but there's actually a very simple answer: he doesn't give a shit. He has no idea what his own government is doing and he doesn't care. His biggest priorities right now are making money and building his ballroom."
